# About Minahil

I'm Minahil, a Computer Science student at the University of Management and Technology (UMT) in Lahore, Pakistan. I'm currently in my 7th semester of the BS Computer Science program.

My main interest is artificial intelligence. I'm exploring deep learning and neural networks, agentic AI and generative AI. Most of my projects so far connect to AI in some way, for example a skin disease detection app, a RAG chatbot, and running a small language model locally on my own laptop.

Besides studying, I work as a video editor and social media manager for a digital agency based in Dubai. I also run a small handcrafted decorative candle business called thecandlescent, where I make custom-packaged candles for occasions like birthdays and weddings.

I like casual, direct communication. When I explain academic topics out loud, I'm most comfortable mixing English and Roman Urdu.

# My opinions, habits and preferences

## How I work
I'm a night owl. I'm more awake and productive late at night than early in the morning, so my best study and work sessions happen after dark. Mornings are not really my thing.

## My view on AI
I think AI should assist people, and humans must always verify what it produces. A model can sound very confident and still be wrong, so I check the output before I trust it. This is also why I like RAG chatbots: they answer from real documents instead of guessing.

## My favourite part of AI
My favourite area of AI is deep learning and neural networks. I also find agentic AI and generative AI really interesting, and I want to keep exploring all three.

## Advice for junior students
Practice over reading. Reading about an algorithm or a tool helps, but you only really learn it when you build something and break it a few times.

## Where I see myself
My dream path is starting my own business. I already run a small handcrafted candle business called thecandlescent, so that is where I am learning the basics.

## Small preferences
I drink neither coffee nor tea. I'm a night person, not a morning person. I like casual and direct conversations, with a bit of humour.

# My projects

## Skin disease detection app (Final Year Project)
My final year project is a skin disease detection app that covers 5 to 6 conditions. It uses the Kaggle DermNet and HAM10000 datasets. The core deliverable is a working app where a user uploads a photo, gets a prediction with a confidence score, can flag a case for a doctor, and can see their scan history. Instead of trying to beat existing accuracy benchmarks, my group is focusing on a deployable app, evaluation broken down by skin tone, and a Pakistan-specific context. Earlier, my group explored manhole and open cover detection, because there is no Pakistan-specific dataset and existing models do poorly on the open or missing class. We moved away from it because our advisor preferred a development-heavy project.

## MindBridge-RAG
MindBridge-RAG is a group project for my cloud computing course: a RAG chatbot for focus and concentration topics. The first version (S1, basic RAG) was tested and got perfect scores in human evaluation. The second version (S2, safety-aware RAG) has not been tested yet. I built the evaluation CSV files and a presentation deck covering the full pipeline.

## Task Manager app (MAD final project)
A mobile app built with React Native, Expo Router and TypeScript, with Supabase as the backend. It uses the OpenWeather API with Pakistani cities, has six database tables and two user roles.

# My study notes: AI search, compilers and cloud

These are notes from my exam preparation in July 2026, written in my own words.

## AI course: search and optimization
Uninformed search explores the problem blindly, while informed search uses a heuristic to guess which state is closer to the goal. Best-First Search always expands the state that looks best by the heuristic alone. Beam Search keeps only the best few states at each level, which saves memory but can miss the optimal path. IDDFS repeats depth-limited depth-first search with a growing limit, so it uses little memory and still finds the shallowest goal. IDA* does the same idea with a cost limit instead of a depth limit.

Hill Climbing moves to the best neighbouring state and stops when no neighbour is better. Its weakness is that it can get stuck in local maxima, plateaus or ridges. For two-player games I studied Alpha-Beta Pruning, which gives the same answer as minimax but skips branches that cannot change the final decision. I also studied constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), the PEAS framework for describing an intelligent agent (Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors), and genetic algorithms, which evolve solutions through selection, crossover and mutation.

## Compiler construction: parsing
LL(1) parsers read the input left to right and build a leftmost derivation using one lookahead symbol. For that to work, left recursion has to be removed from the grammar. CLR(1) parsers use canonical sets of items with lookahead symbols, GOTO transitions and a parsing table. LALR merges CLR(1) states that have the same core to make the table smaller. After parsing, the compiler builds a parse tree or an abstract syntax tree (AST) and generates three-address code (TAC), which can be stored as quadruples, triples or indirect triples. I also practised converting infix expressions to postfix.

## Cloud computing
I studied mobile cloud computing and offloading methods, and AWS services: S3 for object storage, EC2 for virtual servers, RDS and Aurora for relational databases, DynamoDB for NoSQL, ElastiCache for caching and Redshift for data warehousing. Exam questions were scenario-based, where I had to pick the right service for an architecture. I also covered AWS Bedrock and generative AI foundations.
